docs.title: TensorBoard Book
docs.text: tensorboard-book is a web application for organizing and comparing the runs in a TensorBoard log folder. It indexes every run, reports the best value of each scalar, and stores tags, notes, collections and fields alongside the runs.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• A table of all runs with their best scalars, hyperparameters and filters.
  • Tags, notes and stars for each run, collections of runs, and typed fields (numbers with units, choices, dates, links and more) that you define.
  • Comparison of a collection at the step where a selection scalar is best, with mean ± std over seeds and CSV, Markdown or LaTeX export.
  • Overlaid training curves with TensorBoard's smoothing.
  • A timeline of when runs were active, and compute hours per day.
  • A file browser with previews, diffs and downloads for each run.
  • TensorBoard on any selection of runs.

tensorboard-book reads the folder you pass to tensorboard --logdir and never modifies it.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
tensorboard-book [ROOT] [--host 127.0.0.1] [--port 8501] [--depth 1]
                 [--db PATH] [--workers N] [--no-auth] [--no-browser]
                 [--tensorboard-host 127.0.0.1]          scan, then start the app
tensorboard-book view --logdir RUN [RUN ...] [TB args]   TensorBoard on some runs
tensorboard-book scan ROOT [--depth N] [--force]         index without the app (cron)
tensorboard-book hash-password                           create the password hash
tensorboard-book demo [DEST]                             create demo runs
tensorboard-book export-annotations ROOT [-o FILE]       write annotations to JSON
tensorboard-book import-annotations ROOT FILE            merge annotations from JSON
tensorboard-book -v, --version                           print the version

Streamlit prints the address to open. Usage statistics are off, and the app doesn't watch its source files for changes.

Starting the app first scans the folder in the terminal, using up to four processes (--workers), so the page opens with everything indexed. Rescans from the app (the Rescan button and Auto) run inside the app in a single process and only re-read runs that changed. As a rough guide, 300 runs with 6.6 million scalar values (290 MB) take about 35 s with one worker and 18 s with four. An unchanged folder rescans in under a second.

docs.title: Options of each command
docs.text: The output of --help for each command, as installed.

docs.title: tensorboard-book
docs.text:
-v or --version prints the version and the years of the project, for example:

$ tensorboard-book --version
tensorboard-book version 0.9.0 2026

usage: tensorboard-book [-h] [-v]
                        {serve,scan,view,hash-password,demo,export-annotations,import-annotations}
                        ...

Bookkeeping for folders of TensorBoard runs.

positional arguments:
  {serve,scan,view,hash-password,demo,export-annotations,import-annotations}
    serve               start the web app (default)
    scan                index a folder without starting the app
    view                show only some runs in TensorBoard (tensorboard-view)
    hash-password       create the password hash variable
    demo                create a folder of fake runs
    export-annotations  write annotations to JSON
    import-annotations  merge annotations from JSON

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -v, --version         show program's version number and exit

docs.title: tensorboard-book serve
docs.text:
The default command: tensorboard-book ROOT is the same as tensorboard-book serve ROOT.

usage: tensorboard-book serve [-h] [--depth DEPTH] [--db DB]
                              [--workers WORKERS] [--host HOST] [--port PORT]
                              [--no-auth] [--no-browser]
                              [--tensorboard-host TENSORBOARD_HOST]
                              [root]

positional arguments:
  root                  runs folder

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --depth DEPTH         folder depth of runs
  --db DB               database path (default: ROOT/.tensorboard-
                        book/index.db)
  --workers WORKERS     processes used to parse runs (default: up to 4)
  --host HOST           address to listen on
  --port PORT           port to listen on (default: 8501, or the next free
                        one)
  --no-auth             skip the password even if TBOOK_PASSWORD_HASH is set
                        (only with a local --host)
  --no-browser          don't open the app in a browser tab
  --tensorboard-host TENSORBOARD_HOST
                        address for TensorBoards opened from the app (they
                        have no password, so keep it local unless your
                        network is trusted)

docs.title: Password and access
docs.text:
• On 127.0.0.1 the password is optional: the app asks for one only when TBOOK_PASSWORD_HASH is set, and --no-auth skips it anyway. Any other --host needs the hash.
  • The password is checked against a salted hash in TBOOK_PASSWORD_HASH, created with tensorboard-book hash-password. A second hash in TBOOK_VIEWER_PASSWORD_HASH gives read-only access: browsing and downloading, but no edits.
  • Files can only be downloaded from a logged-in session. Links to files outside the runs folder (e.g. symlinks) are refused.
  • To share the app beyond your machine, use an SSH tunnel or a reverse proxy with HTTPS. See Access from another computer.

To create the password hash, see Set a password.

docs.title: Single user
docs.text:
Keep the default --host 127.0.0.1 and reach the app through an SSH tunnel or a private network such as Tailscale:

ssh -L 8501:localhost:8501 you@server

docs.title: Team access over the internet
docs.text:
Keep the app on 127.0.0.1 and put a reverse proxy with HTTPS in front of it. For example, with this Caddyfile:

tbook.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8501
}

Without HTTPS, the password is sent over the network in plain text.

docs.title: Password
docs.text: Only a salted scrypt hash of the password is stored, in an environment variable. Anyone who can read the process environment on the server can see the hash, but the hash does not reveal the password. Each wrong attempt waits one second. To change the password, generate a new hash and restart the app. Open sessions end on restart.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: Files can only be downloaded from a logged-in session, through a random, short-lived link. Paths are checked to be inside the runs folder, so symlinks that point elsewhere are refused. Streamlit's static file serving is enabled only for the fonts bundled with the package. It never serves the runs folder. Do not point another web server at the runs folder.

docs.title: TensorBoard
docs.text:
TensorBoard has no password. TensorBoard instances started from the app therefore listen on 127.0.0.1 by default, and their links work on the machine that runs the app. When the app runs on a server, forward the TensorBoard port as well. The panel in the app shows the command, for example:

ssh -L 6006:localhost:6006 you@server

--tensorboard-host 0.0.0.0 makes the instances reachable from the network. This exposes the selected runs to anyone who can reach that port, so use it only on a trusted network.

docs.title: Large files
docs.text: File previews read at most 300 KB. Zip downloads are limited to 1 GB, which can be changed in Fields and settings → Settings. A single file download is read into memory, so copy very large checkpoints with scp or rsync instead.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer.
  • uv (recommended) or pip.

docs.title: With pip
docs.text:
Install tensorboard-book from PyPI into a virtual environment:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # on Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install tensorboard-book

The tensorboard-book command is available while the environment is active. To upgrade to a newer version, run pip install --upgrade tensorboard-book.

To install the latest code from GitHub instead of the PyPI release:

pip install git+https://github.com/eagomez2/tensorboard-book

docs.title: With uv
docs.text:
uv tool install puts the command in an environment of its own, so it is available everywhere without activating anything:

uv tool install tensorboard-book

docs.title: From a copy of the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/eagomez2/tensorboard-book
cd tensorboard-book
pip install .            # or: uv tool install .

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
tensorboard-book --version

To work on the code instead, see CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Start the app
docs.text:
Pass the folder that contains your runs, the same folder you would pass to tensorboard --logdir:

tensorboard-book /path/to/runs

The command first indexes the folder, then prints the address of the app:

  tensorboard-book 0.9.0

  Runs folder: /path/to/runs
  Database: /path/to/runs/.tensorboard-book/index.db
  Runs: 14 (14 new, 14 parsed)

  You can now view your Streamlit app in your browser.

  URL: http://127.0.0.1:8501
  • Browser. The app opens in a new browser tab. --no-browser turns this off. On a machine without a display, such as over SSH, no tab is opened.
  • Port. The app listens on port 8501, or on the next free port if 8501 is in use. With --port, that exact port is used, and the app stops if it is busy.
  • Address. The app listens on 127.0.0.1 by default, so only the same computer can reach it. Any other --host requires a password.

docs.title: Set a password
docs.text:
Without a password hash, the app does not ask for a password. This is only allowed on 127.0.0.1. To require a password:

  1. Create a password hash. The password itself is never stored.

    tensorboard-book hash-password
# Password: ********
# Repeat:   ********
# TBOOK_PASSWORD_HASH=5c1f…:9ae2…

  2. Set it in the environment and start the app:

    export TBOOK_PASSWORD_HASH='5c1f…:9ae2…'
tensorboard-book /path/to/runs

When TBOOK_PASSWORD_HASH is set, the app asks for the password. --no-auth skips it for one launch, on 127.0.0.1 only. The app does not start if the hash is malformed, or if it is missing while --host is not local.

TBOOK_VIEWER_PASSWORD_HASH, created the same way, sets a second, read-only password. Viewers can browse and download, but not edit.

To reach the app from another computer, see Password and deployment.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: This page walks through tensorboard-book on a demo folder. It assumes that you know TensorBoard and have installed tensorboard-book.

docs.title: 1. Open the demo
docs.text:
tensorboard-book demo tbook-demo    # writes 14 example runs to ./tbook-demo
tensorboard-book tbook-demo         # starts the app on them

The demo is a standard TensorBoard log folder. It contains a learning-rate sweep (resnet_…), an ablation with three seeds per setting (aug_…), a Keras run and two runs that are still active. Some tags, notes, collections and fields (the dataset, the GPU, the parameter count, a rating) are already set.

docs.title: 2. Find the best run
docs.text:
The app opens on Experiments. Each row is a run, with the best value of each scalar. ↑ means higher is better, ↓ means lower is better.

  • Type optimizer.lr < 1e-3 and val/acc > 0.9 in Filter.
  • In the sidebar, set Collection to lr_sweep.
  • Add Params with Show, or filter on it: Params < 20M.

docs.title: 3. Compare an ablation
docs.text:
Open Compare, pick aug_ablation and turn on Aggregate seeds.

Each run is read at the step where val/acc was best, and the other scalars are taken at that same step. Seeds are averaged into mean ± std. You can export the table as CSV, Markdown or LaTeX.

Further down, Which settings lead to the best result works like TensorBoard's HParams dashboard.

docs.title: 4. Look at curves and at one run
docs.text:
• Curves overlays runs, with the same smoothing as TensorBoard, and can draw several scalars on one chart.
  • Run details shows one run. Pick resnet_lr3e-3: the Timing tab shows that it crashed and was resumed. The Overview tab shows its fields, the Artifacts tab its files, and Edit changes its tags, notes and fields.

docs.title: 5. Open TensorBoard
docs.text: For images, histograms and other plugins, tick some rows in Experiments and press Open in TensorBoard.

docs.title: 6. Use your own runs
docs.text:
Stop the demo with Ctrl+C and start the app on the folder that you pass to tensorboard --logdir:

tensorboard-book /path/to/runs

Each folder one level down with event files is a run. Use --depth 2 if your runs are nested deeper. The files in the folder are never modified.

docs.title: Coming from TensorBoard
docs.text: In TensorBoard In tensorboard-book tensorboard --logdir runs tensorboard-book runs Scalars dashboard Curves, and best values in Experiments HParams dashboard Compare → Which settings lead to the best result Run filter (regex) Filter and Search Images, histograms, graphs Open in TensorBoard Tags, notes, collections, fields and Timeline

docs.title: What counts as a run
docs.text:
A run is a folder, one level below the root, that contains events.out.tfevents.* files anywhere inside it:

runs/                     <- tensorboard-book runs
├── resnet_lr3e-4/        <- a run
│   ├── events.out.tfevents.…
│   ├── config.yaml       <- becomes hyperparameters
│   ├── checkpoints/…     <- artifacts
│   └── samples/…
└── keras_baseline/       <- also one run
    ├── train/events…     <- tags become train/epoch_loss, …
    └── validation/events…
  • Event files in subfolders are merged into the run, with the subfolder as a tag prefix (Keras' train/ and validation/). PyTorch's add_hparams timestamp subfolders are merged without a prefix.
  • If your runs are nested deeper, use --depth. For example, with runs/project/exp1/events…, use tensorboard-book runs --depth 2.
  • Both PyTorch-style scalars (simple_value) and TF2 tensor scalars are read.
  • Hyperparameters come from the TensorBoard hparams plugin and from config files. See Config files.
  • Text summaries are shown on the run page. Images, histograms and other plugins are counted but not rendered: open TensorBoard for those. The run page shows the exact tensorboard --logdir … command.

docs.title: Config files
docs.text:
The values of a run's config files become its hyperparameters. A config file is a .yaml, .yml, .json or .toml file whose name matches one of the patterns in Fields and settings → Settings → Config file names. The default patterns are config.*, hparams.*, args.*, params.*, cfg.* and opts.*.

  • A pattern without /, such as train_*.yaml, matches file names at the top of the run, one folder down, or in .hydra/.
  • A pattern with /, such as conf/*.toml, matches the path inside the run, at any depth.
  • Case is ignored.

The first pattern that matches a file of the run gives its main config file. When a run has several config files, the main one wins for keys they share. Run details compares the main config files of two runs even when their names differ, for example config.yaml and exp_42.yaml.

Lightning's hparams.yaml with !!python/object tags is read safely, and nothing is ever instantiated.

docs.title: Renamed, moved, copied and deleted runs
docs.text: Runs are identified by a fingerprint of their first event file, not by their path, so renaming or moving a run folder keeps its tags, notes, fields and collections. A copied folder becomes a new run. A deleted folder is marked Missing and keeps its annotations until you choose Fields and settings → Project → Backup → Forget missing runs. tensorboard-book never modifies or deletes anything in your runs folder, apart from its own two files.

docs.title: Where data is stored
docs.text:
File What Safe to delete? ROOT/.tensorboard-book/index.db SQLite index (WAL mode). Yes. It is rebuilt from the event files, and annotations are restored from the backup below. ROOT/.tensorboard-book/annotations.json Your tags, notes, stars, collections, fields, scalar groups, directions and display, and settings. It is rewritten after every edit. No. Commit it to git or back it up. ROOT/.tensorboard-book/annotations-v1.json A copy of the annotations file as it was before the upgrade from properties to fields. Only there if you used an older version. Yes, once you've checked your fields.

The folder is hidden, so it doesn't clutter the runs folder, isn't taken for a run and doesn't appear in the artifact browser, but it is copied or moved along with the runs folder. Files from versions before 0.6 (ROOT/.tbook.db, ROOT/tbook_annotations.json) are moved into it on the next start.

If the runs folder isn't writable, both files go to ~/.cache/tensorboard-book/<folder name>-<hash>/. You can also choose the location with --db PATH, and the annotations file goes next to it. On first start with an empty database, annotations are restored from the JSON automatically. You can also export and import them from Fields and settings → Project → Backup or with the export-annotations and import-annotations commands.

docs.title: The annotations file
docs.text: The annotations file is version 2. Next to runs, it has fields (the field definitions), tag_options (the order, and so the colors, of the tags), metric_display (each scalar's group, unit, scale and decimals), metric_directions, settings, and the collections, which are still stored under groups. Version 1 files, with properties instead of fields, can still be imported: category properties become choice fields with their values as options, in alphabetical order. See Coming from properties.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Fields are values you add to runs by hand, for things the logs don't say or that you decide afterwards: the dataset, the parameter count, the GPU, a rating, whether someone reviewed the run, a link to the write-up.

Each field has:

  • a name and an optional group (such as Data, Model or Review). Fields of a group stay together everywhere: in the Overview cards, in the Edit form and in Show (Model · params).
  • a type: number, text, choice (one of a list), tags (several of a list), yes/no, date or link.
  • for numbers, a unit, a scale prefix (k, M, G, m, µ, Ki, Mi, …) and decimals for display, and whether higher or lower is better. Values are stored as entered, so 25.6M with scale M shows as 25.6 M and still sorts and filters as 25,600,000. A number that ranks gets ↑ or ↓ in its header and its best value highlighted, like a scalar.
  • for choice and tags, an ordered list of options. An option's place in the list gives its color, so a value keeps its color everywhere. Typing a value that isn't an option yet adds it at the end.
  • a description, shown as help next to its input.

Using them:

  1. Define fields in Fields and settings → Fields.
  2. Give runs values in Run details → Edit, or for many runs at once in Experiments: select rows, then Field in the toolbar.
  3. Show them as columns with Show in Experiments and Compare, filter on them (Dataset == cifar-100, Params < 20M, Rating >= 4) and find them with the sidebar search.

The run tags are the built-in Tags field: its options and colors are managed the same way, and it can't be renamed or deleted. Fields are saved in the annotations backup with everything else.

docs.title: Copy fields to another runs folder
docs.text: Fields and settings → Fields → Export fields saves the field definitions, with their options and the order of the tag options, to tensorboard-book-fields.json (format tensorboard-book-fields). Values are not included. Import fields reads that file, an annotations file (only its fields are used) or a version 1 file with properties. Fields are matched by name: those that already exist are kept as they are, or updated from the file if you choose Update from the file. Updating can change a field's type. Values are never touched.

docs.title: Coming from properties
docs.text:
Before fields, runs had properties, which were either a number or a category. The first time a database with properties is opened, it is upgraded:

  • a number property becomes a number field.
  • a category property becomes a choice field whose options are its values in alphabetical order, so pill colors start out the same.
  • before anything changes, the annotations file is copied to annotations-v1.json next to it, so the previous state is kept.

Annotation files with properties (version 1) can still be imported.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
The Filter box in Experiments takes conditions joined by and:

optimizer.lr < 1e-3 and val/acc > 0.9 and model ~ resnet
  • Keys: hyperparameters (dotted names, as in the table), scalar tags (using the Best/Last value shown), fields (by name, or prop:name if a hyperparameter has the same name), run, status or steps. Wrap keys with spaces in backticks.
  • Operators: == (or =), !=, <, <=, >, >=, and ~ for a case-insensitive regular expression, e.g. run ~ ^aug_.
  • Numbers compare as numbers, everything else as text. A misspelled key gets a "did you mean" suggestion.

The sidebar filters appear in Experiments and Timeline, the views they change, and keep their values while you visit other views:

  • Search looks for text in names, tags, notes and config values.
  • Collection, Tags, Status, Starred only and Show archived narrow down the runs.

Compare can use the same runs through Runs shown in Experiments. Curves and Run details list every run that isn't archived.

docs.title: Scalars and settings
docs.text: Both are in Fields and settings, in the Scalars and Settings tabs.

docs.title: Scalars
docs.text:
Each logged scalar has:

  • a group: the tag up to the last / (val for val/acc), unless you change it.
  • a direction: whether higher or lower is better. Names containing loss, error, mse, mae, wer, fid and similar words default to lower is better, and everything else to higher is better. Each scalar is auto (follows that guess) until you pick higher or lower. Reset all to auto forgets every direction you set. Arrows (↑/↓) in column headers show the current choice.
  • a unit, a scale prefix and decimals, for display.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Notes Active if written to within 300 min (5 h) Status threshold. Pause that splits a run into segments 360 min (6 h) Changing it re-parses every run. Seed pattern [_-]?seed[_-]?\d+ Used to aggregate seeds by run name. Max stored points per curve 5000 Longer curves are downsampled for plotting, always keeping the first, last, min and max points. Best, min, max and last values are always computed from every point. Changing it re-parses every run. Max zip download 1024 MB Max TensorBoards at once 5 Each instance is a separate process. Extra TensorBoard arguments (empty) Added to every launch, e.g. --samples_per_plugin images=100. Config file names config.*, hparams.*, args.*, params.*, cfg.*, opts.* Patterns of the .yaml, .yml, .json or .toml files read as hyperparameters. See Config files.

The Auto toggle in the sidebar rescans every 60 seconds and refreshes the page when something changed.

docs.title: Status and run time
docs.text:
Active or stopped. TensorBoard logs don't record that a run finished, so the status says what can be known:

  • Active: an event was written recently. The default is within the last 5 hours, so a run whose epochs take hours still counts as active. Change it in Fields and settings → Settings.
  • Stopped: nothing written for longer than that. The run may have finished, crashed, or been killed.
  • Missing: the folder is gone. Its annotations are kept.
  • Runs that logged NaN or inf values get a red NaN/inf badge.

Run time:

  • Span: time from the first to the last event.
  • Compute: span minus pauses. A pause is a silence longer than 6 h by default. Set the pause above your longest time between two logged values (e.g. one epoch), or it would cut normal training into pieces.
  • Throughput: steps per second of compute.

docs.title: In more detail
docs.text:
TensorBoard logs have no "finished" marker, so these are estimates from the event timestamps.

  • "Best" is the best logged value, not a smoothed one.
  • Other scalars in Compare use the logged step closest to the best step. If they were logged at different intervals, the step shown may differ slightly.
  • Plotted curves are downsampled above the point limit (the reported numbers are not).
  • Only scalars and text are shown. Images, histograms and other plugins are not shown.

docs.title: Opening TensorBoard
docs.text:
TensorBoard starts TensorBoard on exactly the runs you pick: the selected rows in Experiments (under Open in), the runs being compared in Compare (Open in TensorBoard), or the run shown in Run details (the TensorBoard button). Use it to look at images, histograms and anything else tensorboard-book doesn't show.

  • The run folders are linked (not copied) into a temporary folder, so TensorBoard lists them under the same names.
  • It starts in the background on the first free port from 6006. Press Open in new tab once it's ready. Pressing the button again for the same runs reuses the running TensorBoard.
  • Running TensorBoards are listed below the toolbar with a Stop button. All of them stop when tensorboard-book exits. At most 5 run at once by default (Fields and settings → Settings, which also takes extra TensorBoard arguments).
  • TensorBoard has no password, so it only listens on this machine (127.0.0.1). If you reach tensorboard-book through an SSH tunnel, forward the TensorBoard port too, e.g. ssh -L 6006:localhost:6006 server.

From a terminal, tensorboard-book view --logdir RUN [RUN ...] does the same in the foreground. Any other options are passed to TensorBoard.

docs.title: The views
docs.text:
Pick a view from the menu in the sidebar. The current one is highlighted. The menu has three sections:

  • Explore: Experiments, Run details, Compare, Curves and Timeline.
  • Organize: Collections.
  • Project: Fields and settings, and Help.

Every view is laid out the same way, top to bottom:

  1. The title, with a How this page works button on the right.
  2. Summary cards with the key numbers.
  3. Controls for what to show. Show always adds extra columns.
  4. The content.
  5. Under a table, a row of buttons: how many rows are selected, the actions on them (greyed out until they apply), and the downloads on the right. Charts have a Download figure button that saves them as plotly JSON.

Help, the last item of the menu, is a page with every guide, one topic at a time: the per-view guides, plus filters, status and run time, fields, TensorBoard and password access. The bottom of the sidebar shows how many runs there are and how many are active, when they were last scanned, Rescan and Auto, and the version you're running. The app follows your system's light or dark setting. To pick one, open the ⋮ menu in the sidebar's bottom-left corner and choose Settings → Theme.

The sidebar filters (collection, tags, status, search, starred, archived) only appear in the views they change, Experiments and Timeline, and keep their values while you visit other views. Compare can use the same runs through Runs shown in Experiments. Curves and Run details list every run that isn't archived.

The pages in this section are the same guides the app shows under How this page works:

View What it's for Experiments The main table: every run with its best scalars, filters, tags, collections and fields. Run details Everything about one run: its fields, files, scalars and timing. Compare A fair comparison of a collection, with seeds aggregated and exports for papers. Curves Training curves of up to eight runs, overlaid and smoothed. Timeline When runs were active, how many ran at once, compute hours per day. Collections Named sets of runs, such as a sweep or an ablation study. Fields and settings Fields, scalar display, settings, disk usage and backups.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
Collections are named sets of runs, such as a sweep or an ablation study. A run can be in several collections, and deleting a collection keeps its runs.

  • New collection: a name and an optional description. You can also select runs in Experiments and use Add to collection under the table.
  • Edit collection: rename it, describe it, change its runs, or delete it.
  • Each collection remembers its selection scalar (from Compare) and its scalar columns (from Experiments).

Pick a collection in the sidebar Collection filter to see only its runs, or in Compare to compare them.

Collections used to be called groups. They are still stored under "groups" in the annotations file, so older files import unchanged.

docs.title: Compare
docs.text:
Compares the runs of one collection (an ablation study) fairly.

What to compare. A collection, Selected runs (the runs you ticked before pressing Compare in Experiments), or Runs shown in Experiments (the runs that pass the sidebar filters). Use Show to add tags, notes, status, collections, steps or fields to the table, so you can check that you're comparing the runs you meant to. When seeds are aggregated, a runs column lists the runs behind each row, number fields are averaged and choice fields list their values.

Selection scalar. For each run, the step where this scalar is best is chosen (the "checkpoint"). Every scalar in Scalars at that step is shown at that same step, using the logged value closest to it. That's how test scores should be reported: picking the best test value on its own would be cherry-picking.

Baseline. Pick a run (or, with seeds aggregated, a config) to show each number's difference to it in brackets, e.g. 0.9414 (+0.0147). Green means better and orange means worse, following the scalar's direction. The differences are also in the exports. With None, the default, the table shows no differences.

Aggregate seeds. Collapses runs that differ only by their seed into one row with mean ± standard deviation and the number of runs (n). Two ways to decide that runs share a config:

  • their names match after removing the seed pattern (_seed1, -seed-2, and so on). The pattern is a regular expression that can be edited.
  • all hyperparameters match except the ones named seed.

Below the table:

  • a dot plot of the selection scalar (with error bars when aggregated).
  • What differs between these runs: the hyperparameters that vary, with cells highlighted where they differ from the best run.
  • Which settings lead to the best result: pick a Target scalar and the Settings (hyperparameters and number fields) to see, like TensorBoard's HParams dashboard, a parallel coordinates plot and the target against each setting, with the best run ringed. The parallel coordinates plot has one line per run, colored by the target. Drag along an axis to keep only the runs in that range, or drag an axis name to reorder the axes. Wide-ranging numbers such as learning rates use a log scale, and missing values are shown as a dash.
  • exports as CSV, Markdown or LaTeX (with the best value in bold).

The cards on top show how many runs and configs are compared and which one is best. The selection scalar is saved with the collection.

Open in TensorBoard (under the table) starts TensorBoard on exactly the compared runs. See TensorBoard.

The link in the address bar opens this exact comparison, so it can be shared or bookmarked. It keeps the collection (or the runs, when they aren't one), the selection scalar, the scalars at that step, the Show columns, the seed options and the baseline. Opening it asks for the password first if one is set.

docs.title: Which settings lead to the best result
Curves
docs.text:
Overlays training curves of up to eight runs.

  • Runs and Scalars: one chart per scalar, one line per run. Each run keeps its color while you add or remove others.
  • Smoothing: the same debiased exponential moving average as TensorBoard. The faint line is the raw data.
  • X axis: steps, hours since the run started (to compare speed), or wall time.
  • Log y: logarithmic y axis.
  • Overlay scalars: below the charts, draws several scalars of the chosen runs on one chart, to compare scalars on the same scale (for example train/loss and val/loss). It starts with scalars that share a name after the last /. Color by run or scalar; the other one is told apart by the line style.

Long curves are thinned to at most 5000 points for plotting, always keeping the first, last, lowest and highest points. Values in tables are always computed from every point.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
The main table, with one row per run.

Columns. Pick them in the three boxes at the top:

  • Scalars: the value per run is the best one (highest or lowest, depending on the scalar's direction, shown by ↑ and ↓) or the last one, depending on the Value switch. The best value in each column is highlighted. Your choice is saved per collection.
  • Hyperparameters: by default, the ones that differ between the runs shown.
  • Show: extra columns such as status, steps, compute time, start, tags (as colored pills), collections, notes and your fields. Fields are listed with their group, as Model · params (M); see Fields.

Filter. Narrow the table with conditions, e.g. optimizer.lr < 1e-3 and val/acc > 0.9. See Filters.

Actions. Tick rows and use the buttons under the table. They are greyed out until they apply:

  • Open in: Run details (one run), Curves, or TensorBoard, which starts TensorBoard on the selected runs (see the TensorBoard topic).
  • Compare (two or more runs) opens them in Compare, even if they aren't in a collection.
  • Add to collection adds them to a collection (or a new one) or removes them from the current one.
  • Field sets or clears a field on all selected runs. Pick Tags to add or remove tags.
  • Star and Archive: archived runs are hidden unless you turn on Show archived in the sidebar. Their files are untouched.
  • Export CSV saves the table as shown.

The numbers on top. The number of runs shown, how many are active (see the ⓘ next to Active now), total compute time, and disk usage.

docs.title: Fields and settings
docs.text:
Everything about how this runs folder is described, in four tabs.

  • Fields: the fields you add to runs (see Fields). Edit the table and press Save fields: add a row to create a field, change a name to rename it (its values follow), change its group, type, unit, scale, decimals, direction or options, or untick Visible to keep it out of Show by default. Changing the type converts the values and stops with a message if one doesn't fit. Tick Delete to remove a field and its values when you save. Rename values changes a value on every run that has it: fix a typo, merge two spellings such as resnet and ResNet, reorder (which sets the colors) or delete the values of a choice or tags field, including the built-in Tags. The table only edits the list a field offers, and keeps the values runs still use. Export fields and Import fields copy the definitions to another runs folder; values are not included.
  • Scalars: for each logged scalar, its group (the tag up to the last / unless you change it), whether higher or lower is better, its unit, scale and decimals. Names with loss, error, mse and similar words default to lower; auto follows that guess. Reset all to auto forgets every direction you set.
  • Settings: the active threshold, the pause length, the seed pattern, the stored points per curve, the zip size limit, the TensorBoard limit and extra arguments, and the names of config files. Changing the pause or the points re-parses all runs.
  • Project: where the runs folder and database are, disk usage per run and per collection, and Backup: download or import the annotations JSON, and forget runs whose folders were deleted.

Read-only visitors see the fields and scalars but can't change them.

The Scalars and Settings tabs are described in more detail in Scalars and settings, and fields in Fields.

docs.title: Run details
docs.text:
Everything about one run.

Top. Status, collections, tags and flags, then compute time, wall span, throughput (steps per second of compute), last step, time since the last event, and disk size.

TensorBoard next to the badges opens this run in TensorBoard.

Edit (next to TensorBoard) opens the editor in place of the page: one card per field group, with Tags under General, then the run's collections, star and archive flag, then its notes. Each field has the input of its type: a number (typed in the field's unit, and it can end in a prefix such as 25.6M), a choice or tags list (type a new value to add it as an option), yes/no, a date, a link or text. Add a field defines a new one without leaving the editor. Press Save changes, or Cancel.

Tabs:

  • Overview: the run's fields in cards, one per field group, with units and colored options, then its collections. Empty fields are hidden unless you turn on Show empty fields.
  • Artifacts: every file in the run folder except event files. Select a file to preview it (images, text and config files, CSV/TSV tables, audio, video) and download it. Select several to download a zip. For text files, pick another run to see a diff of the same file. A config file is compared with the config file of the other run, even when the two have different names.
  • Scalars: every scalar with best, best step, last, min, max, number of points and NaN/inf count.
  • Hyperparameters: the flattened config, where each value came from, and the run's main config file. Compare with another run lists the hyperparameters that differ, whatever the names and formats of the two config files, and their line-by-line difference.
  • Text: text summaries (e.g. from add_text).
  • Timing: activity segments and the pauses between them.

The command to open this run in TensorBoard is at the bottom of the Scalars tab.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
Shows when runs were running.

  • Bars: one per run, from its first to its last logged event. Hover for the span, the compute time and the status. Click a bar to open the run. The dotted line is now.
  • Color by: collection, status or tag. A run with several tags takes the color of the first one in the order of the tag options (Fields and settings → Fields → Rename values), and the hover lists all of them. A run in several collections takes the color of the oldest one.
  • Runs at once: how many runs were running at each moment. Useful to spot idle or overloaded machines.
  • Compute hours per day: a calendar of how many hours of runs happened each day. Pauses (see below) are not counted.

The cards on top count the runs in the range, their compute time, the busiest day, and how many are running now.

Span vs compute time. A silence longer than the pause setting (6 h by default) counts as a pause, e.g. a job that crashed and was resumed the next day. Span is first to last event, and compute leaves out pauses. The Timing tab of a run lists its segments.

Times come from the clock of the machine that ran each job and are shown in your time zone. The start is the first logged event, so setup time before it isn't included.
